A shantytown is a poor, overcrowded settlement made up of makeshift homes that people have built themselves — usually from whatever cheap or discarded materials they could find, like scrap wood, corrugated metal sheets, plastic tarpaulins, cardboard, or mud bricks. These are not planned neighbourhoods. They spring up informally, often on the outskirts of large cities, and they typically lack the basic infrastructure that most people take for granted — things like clean running water, sewage systems, electricity, paved roads, and garbage collection.

The word combines "shanty" (a small, crudely built hut or dwelling) with "town" — so the whole meaning is essentially: a cluster or community of such huts, big enough to resemble a town.
What a Shantytown Actually Looks Like

Imagine entering a dense, chaotic maze of small, cramped homes packed closely together with barely any space between them. The structures are often uneven and fragile — roofs that might leak in the rain, walls that do not fully keep out the cold or heat, and floors that may be bare earth. Narrow, unpaved lanes wind between the homes, often muddy after rain. There are no street addresses, no orderly building plans, and no uniform appearance. The settlement seems to grow organically, expanding outward or upward as more people arrive and add onto existing structures.

Shantytowns exist in many parts of the world, but they are most common in developing countries — across Africa, South Asia, Southeast Asia, and Latin America — particularly on the edges of rapidly growing cities. Some of the most well-known examples include:

  • Dharavi in Mumbai, India — one of the largest and most densely populated urban slums in Asia.
  • Kibera in Nairobi, Kenya — one of the largest shantytowns in Africa.
  • Favelas in Brazil — the word used in Brazil for shantytowns, found in cities like Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo.
  • Townships in South Africa — historically established under apartheid, many still reflect the characteristics of shantytowns today.

Each country or region often has its own local name for these settlements (favela in Brazil, bidonville in French-speaking Africa, slum or jhuggi in India, kampung in parts of Southeast Asia), but they all broadly describe the same kind of place that the word "shantytown" captures in English.

Shantytowns do not appear by accident or laziness. They form because of a set of real pressures that push people toward them:

  1. Rural-to-urban migration: People move from villages to cities hoping for jobs, better schools, or escape from poverty, drought, or conflict. When a city grows faster than its housing supply can keep up with, the overflow of people ends up building their own shelters wherever they can.
  2. Extreme poverty: Formal housing — even cheap rental rooms in a city — is simply unaffordable for many people. Building a makeshift home with scrap materials becomes the only practical option.
  3. Lack of government planning or support: When governments fail to invest in affordable public housing or social infrastructure, shantytowns fill the gap.
  4. Displacement: Wars, natural disasters, and forced evictions can displace large numbers of people who then settle informally on the nearest available land.
  5. Land occupation: People sometimes occupy unused or abandoned land — often illegally — and gradually build a community there. Over time, what starts as a few families can grow into a settlement of thousands.

The residents of shantytowns are almost always people at the economic bottom of society — labourers, domestic workers, street vendors, rickshaw pullers, waste collectors, construction workers, and others who perform essential but low-paid work for the city. Many are migrants who have come from rural areas in search of economic opportunity. Despite common misconceptions, most residents are hardworking people trying to survive and improve their lives within very tight constraints. Many have lived in the same shantytown for decades, raising children and building social networks there.

Life inside a shantytown is marked by significant hardship and deprivation, though the degree varies widely:

  • Overcrowding: Many people share a single small room, sometimes entire families.
  • Water: Residents may have to fetch water from a distant communal tap, buy it from vendors at high prices, or use contaminated sources.
  • Sanitation: Open drains, shared or absent toilets, and limited sewage disposal are common, creating serious health hazards.
  • Disease: Poor sanitation and overcrowding make infectious diseases — cholera, tuberculosis, dengue — spread more easily.
  • Fire risk: Structures made of flammable materials packed tightly together are extremely vulnerable to fires, which can destroy entire sections in minutes.
  • Flooding: Shantytowns are often built on land nobody else wants — flood plains, steep hillsides, low-lying areas — making them vulnerable to natural disasters.
  • Insecurity of tenure: Residents often do not own or legally lease the land they live on, so they can face eviction at any time.
  • Limited access to services: Schools, hospitals, and public transport may be distant or inadequate.

That said, shantytowns are rarely purely grim — they often have vibrant markets, strong community bonds, local shops, places of worship, and a rich social life. Residents show tremendous ingenuity and resilience in building lives under difficult circumstances.

You will encounter several words used in overlapping ways, so it helps to understand the distinctions:

  • Slum: A broader, more general term for any densely populated, run-down urban area with poor living conditions. A slum might include old, decayed formal housing that has deteriorated; a shantytown specifically suggests self-built informal structures. All shantytowns are slums, but not all slums are shantytowns.
  • Ghetto: Originally referred to areas where Jewish people were forcibly confined in Europe; later used in American English for poor, segregated urban neighbourhoods. It carries a strong connotation of racial or ethnic segregation, not just poverty. It does not necessarily mean self-built homes.
  • Informal settlement: A neutral, technical term used by planners, researchers, and government officials to describe communities that have grown outside the formal legal and planning framework. It is essentially another name for a shantytown but without any negative or dramatic connotation.
  • Squatter settlement: Refers specifically to the fact that residents are living on land they do not own or have legal rights to — they are "squatting." Many, but not all, shantytowns are also squatter settlements.
How the Word Is Used in Context

Here are some natural example sentences to show how "shantytown" functions in real language:

  • Thousands of families displaced by the flood built a shantytown on the edge of the city.
  • The government promised to replace the shantytown with proper housing but construction has not begun.
  • She grew up in a shantytown on the outskirts of Nairobi and later went on to become a doctor.
  • The documentary showed the daily lives of children living in a shantytown without access to clean water or schools.
  • A fire tore through the shantytown, destroying hundreds of homes in a matter of hours.
The Tone and Connotation of the Word

"Shantytown" is a descriptive word, not an inherently insulting one — but it does carry connotations of poverty, neglect, and informality. Used carefully and factually, it describes a real and important urban phenomenon. Used carelessly, it can reduce complex, living communities to symbols of failure or backwardness, which is why researchers and policymakers sometimes prefer the neutral term "informal settlement." As a learner, being aware of this nuance will help you use the word with appropriate sensitivity.

A shantytown is an informal, self-built settlement of poor-quality homes that grows up — usually on the edge of a city — because people are too poor or too displaced to afford formal housing. It is defined by makeshift construction, overcrowding, and the absence of basic services like clean water, sanitation, and legal land rights. It is a worldwide urban phenomenon shaped by poverty, rapid urbanisation, and inadequate government planning, and it is home to some of the most economically vulnerable people on earth.
